items.title: Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mathematical reasoning
items.content:
Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mathematical reasoning into a form computer proof assistants like Lean can verify—can help.

Last month, Claude completed the first formalized proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, one of the most famous theorems of all time. This was a project experts thought would take many years. It is the largest Lean proof ever written.

Fermat’s Last Theorem was first proven in 1995 by Sir Andrew Wiles, more than 350 years after it was conjectured. Our proof, which totals over 13 million lines of code, provides machine verification. More importantly, it proves over 29,000 other theorems that the proof requires, across many areas of math which had never before been formalized.

We see this as a major step in the long process of firming up the core of mathematical knowledge, building on work from three centuries of mathematicians and hundreds of contributors to Lean and Mathlib. We are optimistic that AI-assisted verification of mathematical proofs will help reduce the burden of refereeing mathematics in an era where more proofs are being produced than ever before.

You can read about the process on our Science Blog: https://t.co/ryYnDEAU6J

And see the complete proof on GitHub: https://t.co/wlYMXYnofz

items.title: How we think about the “wiki incident,” where our agents wrote to several internet sites: it’s past time for us to defin
items.content:
How we think about the “wiki incident,” where our agents wrote to several internet sites: it’s past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.

Historically, we have treated misalignment largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications such as systems cards. This year, we’ve started to see misalignment cause new types of real-world impact.

For the Hugging Face incident, where misalignment led to security impact to us and third parties, we followed a traditional security incident response playbook. We immediately started working with Hugging Face to understand what had happened and also disclosed publicly the very next day. Our investigation continues, and we are continuing to notify parties whom our models impacted in less significant ways.

Prior to the Hugging Face incident, we saw early signs of agents using the internet in unintended ways, as reported in https://t.co/9aiRxk2eUJ, https://t.co/ADjyzwSUGz, and https://t.co/SUV6jZ3Gaz. We considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we’d shared.

Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities. We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks. We’re working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we're working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.

Introducing WeatherNext 3️⃣— our most advanced global weather AI model yet from @GoogleDeepmind and @GoogleResearch

With prediction capabilities that are up to 5x sharper than WeatherNext 2, the model generates a forecast with high spatial resolution in order to catch fast-evolving rainstorms, map local temperature shifts, and even help wind farms predict their power output.
So, how does it do that?

While traditional weather models rely on massive, physics-based supercomputer simulations that can carry a 6-hour forecast lag, WeatherNext 3 leverages live geostationary satellite observations as inputs and trains directly on real-world surface and atmospheric observations.

By pulling this raw satellite data, it’s able to update the global forecast every single hour. And because weather develops at lightning speed, these quick, detailed insights can help bring more localized forecasting to billions of people and local businesses, especially in regions that are historically underserved due to the high costs of traditional weather forecasting models.

items.title: Good old days at OpenAI in 2016: an agent stares at screen pixels, moves a mouse, and books a flight on United. We calle
items.content:
Good old days at OpenAI in 2016: an agent stares at screen pixels, moves a mouse, and books a flight on United. We called it World of Bits, inside OpenAI Universe. 10 yrs later, Astra is reincarnated in the same universe. Even the naming is astronomically correct 😆

Universe was perhaps the most ambitious AI infra project at the time, but we couldn't quite figure out how to solve it. A policy with zero prior knowledge of what a "submit" button does has to rediscover the entire internet visual lingua by trial and error. In retrospect, RL from scratch against hand-drawn, per-task "artisan" reward functions on a bunch of Pascal Titan X GPUs was completely doomed.

To solve computer use agent, the right way turns out to be boiling the ocean first (hillclimb on every general task you can find), and then specialize back down to the screen pixels and keystrokes. Or simply, a "Specialized Generalist". 
 
Lessons learned: one step ahead of everyone, you're a pioneer. Three steps ahead, you're a prophet. Five steps ahead, you're a martyr.

Congrats, GPT-6! That United flight finally gets booked, reliably this time. The 2016 intern in me has a big smile.

I think building a crowd sourced niche dataset is one of the most UNDERRATED bootstrapped businesses in the AI AGE:

(think LevelsFYI, Glassdoor, Zillow etc but for any niche)

1. Your users build it for you by adding their own data (it gets more valuable with every entry)

2. AI agents now need clean, trusted data to make decisions, and they'll pay to query it on repeat

3. Cloudflare (and others!) are building the rails for agents to pay per query, so this becomes real recurring revenue

4. One dataset sells to many buyers at once: consumers, companies, and now agents

5. Charge three ways from the same data: free for contributors, paid for pros, API access for the agents

6. The narrower the niche, the more defensible it gets (you own a corner nobody else has)

7. Frontier models are hungry for data (and are a great customer)

8. The wedge: give a teaser amount of data, then make people add theirs to unlock the rest (ask for data or email)

9. LevelsFYI was brilliant because people will hand over their own salary just to see what everyone else makes (human nature)

Big fan of these types of businesses in the AI age. 

Low risk, high margin, and they get stronger the longer they run!

This is very similar to how we think about context management in Deep Agents: compaction should reduce what is sent to the model, not erase the underlying work history.

 In Deep Agents, the logic is:

 - every agent gets a filesystem to work with (can be real or virtual)
 - when a tool result is too large, we write the full result to the filesystem (/large_tool_results) and replace the model-visible message with a preview
 - when the conversation gets long, we offload older messages to the filesystem (/conversation_history) history first, then generate a summary
 - the agent can also decide to compact proactively via a compact_conversation tool, which uses the same offload + summarize logic

One non-model thing I'm very excited we announced today with Fable 5.1 is Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS).

Even if you're not a CEO/CISO, this blog post is a look into how big companies are thinking about AI adoption which is important to understand if you're interested in how AI might diffuse across industry.

Companies are giving agents more and more access to internal systems. With traditional zero data retention, there's been no way to spot patterns in what agents might be doing across sessions on these systems.

EFS is ZDR++. It's ZDR built for a world with agents. A company's data stays in its own cloud, and an automated monitoring layer we built flags risky patterns to its team.

I think of this as an observability and risk mitigation layer for agents. My guess is it will become a standard requirement from enterprises for running increasingly powerful AI on their systems.

items.content:
At the core of AI, you really just need:

1) a thing that does
2) connections into tools
3) a place to hold stuff
4) a spot to share and update

In slot 1, we're talking AI agents like Codex or Claude Code or GrokBot. Whether you have a daily driver or a mix and match, doesn't matter. Just an LLM-based system that can spin up hundreds or thousands of agents across multiple tasks at once.

In slot 2, we're talking toggling them toggles and connecting Codex to places like Gmail, Stripe, Magnific, Remotion, web browser, computer use, etc. Your risk tolerance will determine how many toggles you toggle. I now feel comfortable with both Codex and Claude Code having access to my GDrive, Fireflies, etc. and did not feel comfortable when the tool connections first came out.

In slot 3, when AI creates a document or a dashboard, where is it? This could be Google Drive, Dropbox, GitHub, your local storage, Obisidian. But it needs to be a place for your agents to build up their artifacts, task managers, and brain. Their memory. The more multiplayer your system is, the more IAM and cloud matter (aka local storage won't cut it).

In slot 4, you need a hub. When AI completes tasks for you or wants to ask you something, where is it doing that? I use Slack as my team's hub and we have enabled Claude Tag and built our own Claude Code apps as well. 

Am I missing anything? Let me know.

Most teams can tell you what their agent does.

Very few can tell you what it is allowed to do.

Different questions. Th
items.content:
Most teams can tell you what their agent does.

Very few can tell you what it is allowed to do.

Different questions. The second is the expensive one.

Agent integrations usually run through a service account, and that account tends to hold generous permissions, because narrowing them is fiddly and everything works fine while they are wide.

So the agent can reach far more than the task needs.

Nobody decided that. It arrived by default.

Role-based access control is a must for this. Scope the agent to whoever triggered it, resolved at runtime, not a static account holding keys to everything.

Second reason, nothing to do with security: hand a model too many available actions and it gets worse at choosing between them. You burn context on options it never uses. A narrow scope is not only safer. It performs better.

So what should you ask your team this week?

Not what your agents do. What they could do today, if one of them decided to.

Everyone wants to know whether their agent scores an 8 out of 10.

That is the wrong number to watch.

The score alone t
items.content:
Everyone wants to know whether their agent scores an 8 out of 10.

That is the wrong number to watch.

The score alone tells you little. Quality is subjective and it moves with the task. 70% similarity is fine for a marketing draft and unacceptable in a regulated process. There is no universal bar.

What matters is the deviation.

Your system holds steady around a seven. You ship a change. It drops to a five.

Something happened. That is the signal. The deviation matters more than the number itself.

Which makes evals more practical than teams expect. You do not need everyone to agree what a ten means. You need a consistent measure and a baseline you trust.

And you are almost never automating from thin air. There is an existing process, so examples of good already exist in your business. That is your test suite.

After that it is regression testing. New model, new prompt, check the outputs still land where they used to.

So what should you watch?

The drift.

items.content:
One of the best markets to be building for is boomers. Mobile apps, desktop apps, agents, even hardware.

There are 70 million-plus seniors in the US and almost nobody is building for them. 

AI is good at the exact things they need help with: hearing, mobility, memory, vision, and loneliness.

Widen it down to 45 and it gets better. It won't be explosive growth. 

But if you want to build something that makes a couple of million, the people over 45 are the highest earners, they've built up the most savings, their kids have moved out, and they have the free time.

Here's the setup:

1) Pick a category that only gets built for young people. Gaming, dating, fitness, anything with a cooler younger audience.

2) Find the pain point the older version has. Hearing, mobility, memory, vision, loneliness.

3) Build the older version of it. A 55-year-old isn't twitch-fast anymore and gets left out of anything competitive, so build the one you play for the fun of it.

4) Keep the gray hair and the balding off the landing page. They don't see themselves that way. They want a product that makes them happier and healthier.

5) Advertise on Facebook. People will tell you Facebook is dead. It's alive, just not in your age range, and a 55-year-old will hear about you and buy the same day.

6) Leave the targeting off and watch who buys.

This gets better in 10 years.

Gaming is getting more expensive and that whole audience is aging, so the people who can afford to play will be the older ones. 

Dads of Marathon exists. Nobody has built Grandpas of Marathon.

Pick the category, build the older version, then let the ads tell you who's buying

How to actually use (the new) ChatGPT-Astra-6:

1. Do not use ChatGPT in a browser.
2. Download the ChatGPT app first.
3. You must only use Work or Codex modes.
4. The only best effort for Astra is clearly "Medium".
5. Medium sits at the best intelligence + cost + speed.

To make it simpler, go to ChatGPT Work → GPT-6 Astra → Medium.

But instead of reading this post. Go to https://t.co/WWdSxBzs3J to read my full guide (& the exact prompts) on ChatGPT & Claude.

You don't have access to GPT-6 if you are on a free ChatGPT account.

You can think of switching from Claude to ChatGPT:

> GPT-6 is smarter than Fable-5.1.
> GPT-6 is 2x cheaper than Fable-5.1
> And GPT-6 is also 2x faster.

Then prompt gpt-6 like this:

PROMPT TIP 1. Give it a finish line.
"Help me analyze this" has too many gaps to fill.
Instead, state what you actually want to get by the end of the session: a ranked list, a spreadsheet, a finished deck.

PROMPT TIP 2. Decide which questions it may ask.
Astra asks for clarification more than older models (it's a good thing).
Clearly tell the decisions that need to be in your input. It handles the rest.

PROMPT TIP 3. Tell it what each file is for.
Evidence? Template? Style reference?
A simple one-liner explanation will save back-and-forth clarifying chat.

PROMPT TIP 4. Tell it what readable means.
I always add this in my prompts: "Use ASD-STE100." to receive uncomplicated answers.

PROMPT TIP 5. Interrupt Astra mid-task with a new instruction. It updates the plan from there & keeps going.

Mind you: you can't access GPT-6-Astra on a free tier whatsoever.
OpenAI is serving Pro users first, and then Plus users eventually.

One of the best categories to build in right now is pet health.

3) Do the same thing with hardware. Pull up the pet devices that already exist and ask how you inject an AI brain into this to make it a better product.

4) Collars are the easy one. Heart rate, step count, sleep, and a report that goes back to the owner.

There are products already. I'm on PetPaste right now, and Whistle and a few others have added AI recently. 

It's really, really early. Almost nobody I know is using this stuff yet.

Do this one if you love pets. I think it's a no-brainer category.

Find the human product, make the pet version, then put a brain in it

How do you sell agents before you build them?

You run the pilot as labor. You charge for the outcome.

Pick one niche. 

Start with 3 customers with the same workflow and the same pain

Then promise a result you can measure: "we will answer and qualify your missed calls."

Price it simply:
- $1,500 setup, then $1,000 per month for one workflow
- $2,000 setup, then $30 per qualified appointment
- $3,000 per month for up to 500 handled tickets

The exact price matters less than what you learn.

Watch where the agent breaks, what needs approval, and what the customer will miss if you remove it.

Every roofer asks for the same emergency call script, service area check, financing answer, and estimate follow-up. Build the product from that pattern.

Do the work first that's how you earn the software.

How do you get a boring business to trust an AI agent?

Show the test results before you pitch.

Here's an example: The agent handles maintenance requests for property managers.

Take 50 of their old requests. Mark the correct answer for each one. Run the agent against all 50.

Then say this on the call:

"We tested this on 50 of your old maintenance requests. It routed 42 correctly, flagged six of them for human review, and made two mistakes. Here are the two mistakes, and here's how we fix them."

The two mistakes build the trust. The owner believes the 42 because you showed the 2.

Those same 50 examples are also your "gym." Change the prompt, the model, the tools, or the workflow, and the agent goes back through them.

The catch is the order. You build the test set first. Then you promise autonomy.

How to go from zero to Claude pro SEO user in 10 mins: 

The setup is what separates $0 results from $100k results.

1. Load your business brain.

Before anything else paste this into Claude:

"Here is everything you need to know about my business:

[name], [website], [location], [services], [target cities], [top 3 competitor URLs].

Use this as context for everything. Never ask me for this again."

Claude stops being generic. Starts being yours.

Most people skip this and spend the next 6 months getting advice that could apply to any business in any city in any industry.

That's not SEO. That's guessing.

2. Pick the right model.

Open Cowork. Select Opus 4.7. Turn on Extended Thinking.

Most people are running SEO prompts on Sonnet or the default model.

Wrong model = surface level output. Every single time.

Opus 4.7 with Extended Thinking doesn't just answer your question.

It thinks through your entire market before responding.

The difference between a $20/month result and a $ 10k / month agency result is often just this one setting.

3. Set your SEO mission once. Forever.

Go to Settings → Cowork → Edit Global Instructions.

Paste this:

"You are my local SEO strategist with 14 years of experience. Always read my business context before responding.

Always compare my business against my competitors before giving advice. Always prioritise commendations by revenue impact. Never give generic SEO advice that doesn't apply to my specific market and location."

You set this once. It runs every single session.

Your prompts can now be 10 words long and hit harder than a 500 word prompt ever could.

4. Build your competitor file.

Create a document called COMPETITORS.md

Inside list your top 5 competitors with:

- their website URL
- their GBP URL
- their review count and average rating
- the keywords they rank for that you don't
- the categories they have that you're missing

Paste this into Claude before every audit.

Claude now knows exactly who it's competing against.

Every recommendation it makes is built around beating these specific businesses in your specific market.

5. Set your keyword intent filter.

Before running any keyword research tell Claude this:

"Only give me keywords with clear buyer intent. Ignore informational keywords.

Focus only on service + city, emergency + service, and near me combinations. Every keyword you suggest must indicate someone who is ready to call or book today."

This alone eliminates 90% of the wasted SEO effort most businesses do.

6. Before every Claude SEO session check these:

Am I in Cowork not Chat?

Is Opus 4.7 + Extended Thinking on?
Did Claude read my business context?
Is my competitor file loaded?
Is my keyword intent filter set?

Get all five right first. Then run your prompts.

The businesses that do this setup properly are outranking competitors who have been established for years.

The ones that skip it are still getting generic advice and wondering why nothing is moving.

Most people will read this and do nothing.

The ones who set this up today will look back in 90 days and not believe what changed.

Full prompt system in the article below.

Bookmark it.

Give it to Claude.

Right now.

→ see which way BTC is moving
→ follow the move

Microsoft Foundry brings the next stage together: model selection, deployment, agents, tools, tracing, evaluation, and monitoring.

→ Embeddings, vector indexes, and similarity search
→ Azure AI Search and hybrid retrieval
→ Retrieval-augmented generation
→ Agent instructions, state, grounding, and tool use
→ MCP servers and multi-agent workflows

The final destination is production readiness.

That means CI/CD, agent deployment, autoscaling, cost monitoring, observability, content safety, guardrails, prompt-injection defense, groundedness testing, and continuous evaluation.

Learning Azure AI is not about collecting service names.

Let's explore the protocol that became a chain's financial infrastructure. 👇

⚪ Aerodrome at a Glance

Marketplace Insight: Aerodrome has done what almost no DEX outside Uniswap has managed, becoming genuinely essential infrastructure for a major chain. The sharpest evidence arrived in August, when Coinbase launched tokenized US equities on Base and Aerodrome provided the liquidity on day one, clearing $200M in cumulative volume within weeks across Nvidia, Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, and SpaceX. Those pools trade through weekends when traditional exchanges are closed and still track tightly to Monday's open. The clean contrast is between a protocol that has clearly won its position and a token model still being rebuilt to pay for itself, which is precisely what the Aero upgrade sets out to fix.

⚪ Mission

Aerodrome exists to be the liquidity layer a blockchain runs on rather than an application sitting on top of it. The ve(3,3) argument is that liquidity is a market like any other, so instead of the protocol deciding which pools get incentives, token holders who lock for the long term should direct them, and projects wanting deep liquidity should compete for those votes. The result is a marketplace where emissions flow toward whatever the people with the longest time horizons believe is most valuable, aligning incentive spending with genuine demand.

🔵 A Brief History

Aerodrome launched on Base on August 28, 2023, built by Dromos Labs, the same team behind Velodrome on Optimism. The design was deliberate rather than opportunistic: Base needed a primary liquidity layer, and Dromos brought a ve(3,3) model already battle-tested on another Superchain network. The protocol accumulated over a billion dollars in deposits quickly and established dominance that has not since been seriously challenged.

The token launched with 500 million supply, 450 million of it distributed directly as vote-locked veAERO rather than liquid tokens, which set the locking culture from day one. Emissions began at 10 million weekly and moved through a take-off phase of rising emissions, a cruise phase of steady decay, and finally into Aero Fed, the mechanism that handed monetary policy to veAERO voters once weekly emissions fell below 9 million.

The product expanded alongside. Slipstream added concentrated liquidity derived from Uniswap V3, giving LPs the capital efficiency of ranged positions. The Flight School programme ran until April 2026, using protocol revenue to buy and lock tokens as bonuses for new lockers, deliberately growing the locked base before folding into the Public Goods Fund.

2026 has been the most consequential year. Liquidity migrated to MEV-resistant pools from May, and the largest change is structural: Dromos is merging Aerodrome and Velodrome into Aero on MetaDEX03, a single liquidity layer spanning Base, Optimism, Ethereum, Circle's Arc, Unichain, and Celo, with existing AERO and veAERO holders receiving roughly 94.5% of the new supply and locks migrating with amounts and durations intact.

The full launch codebase was published on 30 August, formal audits from ChainSecurity and Sherlock returned no critical or high-severity findings, and a $400,000 Sherlock public audit contest opened on 31 August ahead of a September launch. Alongside it came the clearest validation yet: on 24 August, Coinbase launched tokenized US equities on Base and Aerodrome provided day-one liquidity, followed by Amazon, Microsoft, Strategy, Tesla, and SpaceX on 4 September, with cumulative volume passing $200M.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea is that liquidity direction should be a market, and everything is built to make that market efficient.

➛ The ve(3,3) flywheel. Holders lock AERO into veAERO for up to four years, vote on which pools receive emissions, and collect the trading fees and external incentives from the pools they back, so governance participation and revenue are the same act.

➛ Tokenized equities infrastructure. The primary on-chain venue for Coinbase's tokenized US stocks, providing day-one liquidity across Nvidia, Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, and SpaceX, with pools trading through weekends when traditional markets are closed and tracking tightly to Monday's open.

➛ The AER and REV Engines. Aero introduces dynamic reward rates set per pool by projected revenue and productivity, targeting 8-12% global inflation with a 20% cap, alongside a revenue engine that expands income sources across trading fees, bridge and aggregator fees, launch payments, and MEV, with 100% flowing to AERO stakers.

➛ Predictive Allocation and Metaswaps. Real-time reward allocation by stakers based on expected future demand rather than weekly retrospective votes, with gauge caps and automation, plus a cross-chain aggregator, bridge, and DEX in one interface.

➛ The bribe marketplace. Projects wanting deep liquidity either accumulate veAERO themselves or pay voters to direct emissions their way, creating genuine competitive demand for the token from protocols rather than speculators.

➛ Cross-chain expansion. The Aero merger unifies liquidity across Base, Optimism, Ethereum, Circle's Arc, Unichain, and Celo, with Aerodrome slated to provide day-one liquidity when Arc reaches mainnet.

⚪ Token Utilities

$AERO is a governance and revenue-claim token where locking is the primary action.

➛ veAERO locking: holders lock AERO for up to four years to receive voting power, with longer locks earning proportionally greater influence.

➛ Emission direction: holders allocate AERO emissions across pools, making the token the control mechanism for the entire incentive system.

➛ Fee and incentive claims: voters receive trading fees from the pools they support plus external incentives offered by projects seeking emissions, with the REV Engine routing 100% of protocol revenue to stakers.

➛ Collateral utility: AERO is accepted as collateral for fixed-rate borrowing on Tenor OTC, extending its use beyond the protocol itself.

⚪ Key Features

➛ Dominant position on Base with 50% to 60% of network DEX volume.

➛ Day-one liquidity venue for Coinbase's tokenized US equities.

➛ A ve(3,3) model where roughly 51% of supply is locked at an average of 3.7 years.

➛ The AER Engine tying emissions to projected productivity with a hard 20% cap.

➛ Slipstream concentrated liquidity plus MEV-resistant pool designs.

➛ A cross-chain merger with Velodrome spanning six networks.

🔵 Meet the Team

Aerodrome is built and maintained by Dromos Labs, and the structure is worth stating plainly: this is a protocol whose individual builders are not publicly identified.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Alexander Cutler [ @wagmiAlexander ] - Co-Founder and CEO | Leads Dromos Labs and is the most visible public voice of the protocol, driving the MetaDEX architecture across both Velodrome and Aerodrome and now the merger into Aero. He has overseen a run of shipped upgrades including Slipstream, MEV-resistant pools, and Predictive Allocation.

➛ Luis A. de la Cerda [ @taowatts ] - Co-Founder and Executive Director | Co-founded Dromos Labs and owns the strategic and operational side of the business, including the ecosystem relationships behind Aerodrome's position as Base's primary liquidity layer and its role in the Coinbase tokenized equities launch.

➛ Dromos Labs | The development entity behind both Aerodrome and Velodrome, and the designer of the MetaDEX architecture underpinning them. It manages the development wallet and drives the technical roadmap including Slipstream, Predictive Allocation, and the Aero merger. Individual founders and executives are not publicly disclosed, which for a protocol handling this volume removes a layer of accountability, though the team has an unusually long track record: Velodrome has operated on Optimism since 2022 and Aerodrome since 2023, both without a protocol-level exploit.

➛ veAERO governance | The load-bearing decision-making body. Holders locking roughly 51% of supply at an average of 3.7 years direct emissions, shape monetary policy, and receive the protocol's revenue. Governance here is economic rather than advisory, since votes determine where every emitted token goes.

➛ The Public Goods Fund | Runs programmatic, market-aware buybacks and max-locks, with recent purchases in the hundreds of thousands of AERO monthly, and absorbed the voting power of the concluded Flight School programme in April 2026. Under Aero it becomes the Momentum Fund, formalizing rules-based buybacks, burns, and strategic liquidity.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★⯪ (4.5/5). Aerodrome is genuinely essential infrastructure rather than one venue among many. It handles 50% to 60% of all Base DEX volume, led 54% of BTC-USD volume across every EVM chain in July 2026, has facilitated over $9 billion in cross-border FX swaps, and became the primary on-chain venue for tokenized US equities, clearing $200M in cumulative volume within weeks of Coinbase's launch. That last role is the strongest evidence of all, since it is the kind of function a chain's core liquidity layer earns rather than claims. The 0.5-point deduction is concentration and competition. Aerodrome's fortunes remain tied to Base's growth, the DEX category is contested by Uniswap, Curve, and PancakeSwap, all larger, and the cross-chain expansion through Aero is a serious but unproven attempt to escape single-chain dependency.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★★ (4/5). The locking behaviour is genuinely remarkable, with roughly 51% of total supply committed at an average of 3.7 years, a conviction signal almost nothing in DeFi matches, and the Public Goods Fund has run consistent market-aware buybacks and max-locks totalling hundreds of thousands of AERO in recent months. What lifts this further is that Aero directly addresses the model's weakness: the AER Engine sets reward rates dynamically per pool against projected revenue and productivity, targeting 8-12% global inflation with a hard 20% cap, replacing open-ended emissions with something tied to output, while the REV Engine routes 100% of a widened revenue base to stakers and the Momentum Fund formalizes buybacks and burns. The 1-point deduction is that supply remains uncapped, historical inflation ran near 24.8%, and recent epochs showed net income turning negative at -$400K and -$586K, so the redesign is credible but has not yet proven it closes the gap.

➛ Audits: ★★★★⯪ (4.5/5). The security work ahead of the Aero launch is among the most thorough in this series. Formal audits from ChainSecurity and Sherlock, both top-tier named firms, returned no critical or high-severity findings, supplemented by an additional model-powered review. The full launch codebase was published openly on 30 August across public repositories, and a Sherlock public audit contest with a $400,000 prize pot opened on 31 August, one of the larger bounty pools in DeFi. Underneath that, the protocol inherits a codebase running on Optimism since 2022 and Slipstream derived from Uniswap V3, with Aerodrome itself operating since 2023 at over a billion in TVL without a protocol-level exploit. The 0.5-point deduction is that the contest was still running at time of writing and the merged cross-chain architecture has no production history yet.

➛ Community: ★★★★ (4/5). The lock data is the community's strongest argument. Roughly 51% of supply committed for an average of 3.7 years is not a farming community, it is a base that has voluntarily surrendered liquidity for years in exchange for governance and revenue. Governance is genuinely economic, with holders directing every emitted token, and protocols across Base compete actively for those votes. The Flight School programme deliberately cultivated that locker base before concluding in April 2026, and developer activity is visible in AI-agent tooling like Bankr and the Sugar SDK. The 1-point deduction is that the anonymous team limits the community identity that visible founders tend to build, and a meaningful share of participation is yield-motivated rather than conviction-driven, which the negative net income epochs will test.

🔵 Conclusion

Aerodrome won its market decisively, and August proved how much that position is worth. When Coinbase brought tokenized US equities onto Base, Aerodrome provided the liquidity on day one, and within weeks those pools had cleared over $200 million across Nvidia, Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, and SpaceX, trading through weekends when the underlying exchanges are shut. More than half of all decentralized trading on Base runs through the protocol, and roughly half its token supply is locked for an average of nearly four years.

The bull case is unusually well-evidenced. Aerodrome is not competing for relevance, it already has it, and the Aero upgrade is a serious attempt to fix the one thing genuinely broken: the AER Engine ties emissions to projected productivity with a hard cap, the REV Engine widens the revenue base and routes all of it to stakers, and the whole thing ships behind ChainSecurity and Sherlock audits with a $400,000 contest on top.

Aerodrome already proved it can own a chain's liquidity and become the venue where tokenized stocks trade. What comes next is whether the rebuilt economics finally pay for themselves.
